studies.title: Brain training for burnout still pays off four and a half years later
studies.ns_score_reason: a rare, very long follow-up of a randomized trial in burnout patients, dented by heavy attrition.
studies.the_study: Swedish researchers followed up patients treated at a stress-rehabilitation clinic for exhaustion disorder (clinical burnout), who had been randomized to standard multimodal rehabilitation alone or with added computerized cognitive training (CCT) or aerobic training. Of the original 132 participants, 56 returned 4.5 years later for cognitive testing. The group that had done cognitive training still showed better global cognitive performance, better episodic memory and better performance on a trained working-memory updating task, with scores stable between the one-year and 4.5-year assessments; the exercise group showed no lasting cognitive advantage. Apparent long-term gains in burnout, anxiety and work ability were, the authors say, more plausibly explained by who chose to come back than by the interventions.
studies.why_it_matters: Cognitive problems are the symptom burnout patients most often say lingers after they feel "recovered," and this is among the longest follow-ups showing that a short course of computerized training may leave a durable trace — while also being refreshingly honest that the mood and work-ability findings probably do not.
studies.pitch_angle: Brain-training apps have a terrible reputation for transfer and durability — yet here, nearly five years on, burnout patients who did a few weeks of computerized training were still measurably sharper than those who did rehabilitation alone, while the ones who did aerobic exercise were not. Open on the exhausted knowledge worker who returns to the office and finds they can no longer hold a meeting agenda in their head. Call Hanna Malmberg Gavelin at Umeå University, who has run both the original trial and this follow-up and is unusually candid about which of her own results don't hold up.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a business or work-focused outlet on what actually happens to the brain in clinical burnout, and why Sweden is one of the only countries to treat "exhaustion disorder" as a formal diagnosis with dedicated rehabilitation clinics — including what the rest of the world could learn or should be wary of.
studies.caveats: Small N at follow-up (56 of 132 returned), single clinic, substantial selective attrition that the authors themselves flag as confounding the psychological outcomes, secondary long-term analysis of an earlier trial, some self-reported outcomes.

studies.title: Rapid brain stimulation cuts suicidal thoughts within days in a small trial
studies.ns_score_reason: striking effect sizes and a clinically urgent target, badly limited by no control group and 34 patients.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Thirty-four inpatients with depression — 17 unipolar, 17 bipolar — completed a five-day accelerated course of intermittent theta-burst stimulation (iTBS), a fast form of transcranial magnetic stimulation. Suicidal ideation, behavior and risk were rated daily on the Columbia scale and again at one month. By the end of the week, 97% had responded and 74% were in remission for suicidal ideation; at one month, roughly three-quarters still met response criteria, and bipolar and unipolar patients did about equally well.
studies.why_it_matters: Almost nothing in psychiatry reduces suicidal thinking within days, and the inclusion of bipolar patients — usually excluded from stimulation trials over switch risk — is unusual. But with no sham arm, this is a signal to test properly, not a result to act on.
studies.pitch_angle: The gap between walking into an emergency department with suicidal thoughts and an antidepressant starting to work is measured in weeks. Here it was measured in days — in bipolar as well as unipolar patients. Frame it honestly as an open-label result that needs a sham-controlled replication, and use it as a peg for the wider push toward accelerated TMS protocols; worth calling groups running sham-controlled accelerated iTBS trials in suicidality to ask what effect size survives a placebo condition.
studies.wider_angle: A specialist health-policy piece on why five-day "accelerated" stimulation protocols could reshape psychiatric inpatient care and insurance coverage — compressing six weeks of daily hospital visits into one admission — and what the evidence base would need to look like before health systems pay for it.
studies.caveats: Small N (34), no control or sham group, single center, open-label so expectancy effects are uncontrolled, short follow-up (one month), inpatient sample may not generalize.

studies.title: Short-acting psychedelics are being tested against depression — and one version leaves out the trip
studies.ns_score_reason: timely synthesis of a fast-moving field, but it's a review, and the most interesting compound has no human data at all.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: A systematic review of 51 publications on three tryptamines: DMT, 5-MeO-DMT, and zalsupindole, a putatively non-hallucinogenic analogue. Intravenous DMT's acute effects resolve in 20–30 minutes and sublingual 5-MeO-DMT has a half-life of about 28 minutes; both have been linked to rapid drops in depressive symptoms, and an inhaled 5-MeO-DMT formulation (GH001) hit its primary endpoint in a Phase 2b treatment-resistant depression trial. Zalsupindole's evidence is a single preclinical study showing antidepressant-like effects and neuroplasticity markers without the head-twitch response that signals hallucinogenic activity in rodents.
studies.why_it_matters: The practical obstacle to psychedelic therapy is the eight-hour supervised session; compounds that act in half an hour — or that may separate the plasticity from the trip entirely — would change what a psychedelic clinic even looks like.
studies.pitch_angle: The central question in psychedelic medicine is whether the hallucinations are the treatment or a side effect, and this review lays out the state of the evidence for the drugs designed to answer it — including one candidate with no human data whatsoever. Lead on the contrast between a day-long psilocybin session and a 20-minute inhalation. Roger McIntyre at the University of Toronto is the senior author and will talk; note his extensive industry ties, including Atai Life Sciences, in the piece.
studies.wider_angle: A business and regulation story for a pharma or finance outlet on the race to patent "non-hallucinogenic psychedelics" — who owns what, how regulators would even evaluate a drug whose predecessor's efficacy may depend on subjective experience, and what happens to the therapy-plus-drug business model if the trip is engineered out.
studies.caveats: Systematic review, not primary research; evidence base is thin and heterogeneous; zalsupindole data are animal-only; several key trials are industry-sponsored; senior author declares consultancy and speaker fees from numerous pharmaceutical companies including psychedelic developers.

studies.title: Whether war damages your mental health may depend on what you already believed about the world
studies.ns_score_reason: a clean, human moderation effect in a real-world crisis, limited by cross-sectional self-report.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Six weeks after the start of the Israel-Hamas war, 326 Israeli parents of children aged 3 to 6 (mean age 36.8) completed an online survey covering their exposure to missile attacks, their "world assumptions" — core beliefs about whether the world is benevolent, meaningful and the self worthy — and symptoms of depression and somatization. Exposure to missile attacks was strongly associated with depression and physical symptoms among parents holding negative world assumptions; among those with more positive assumptions, the link was far weaker.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests the psychological damage done by a threat is filtered through pre-existing beliefs rather than being a direct function of how much shelling you experienced — a testable target for intervention, though cross-sectional data cannot tell us which came first.
studies.pitch_angle: Two parents in the same stairwell during the same siren can emerge with very different mental health, and this study points at the reason: their prior assumptions about whether the world is fundamentally benign. Open on a parent counting down sirens with a four-year-old. Call Lee Greenblatt-Kimron at the University of Haifa, and ask the obvious hard question — whether a benevolent worldview protects you, or whether the people who still hold one are simply the people who were doing better anyway.
studies.wider_angle: A longer feature for a current-affairs or international outlet on the psychology of raising small children under bombardment — including Gaza, Ukraine and Sudan — and on how little of the research on "shattered assumptions," a theory built largely in Western peacetime samples, has been tested where the assumptions are actually being shattered.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional and observational (cannot establish causation or direction), entirely self-reported, non-probability online convenience sample, single national population during an acute crisis so may not generalize, no baseline measures of pre-war beliefs or mood.

studies.title: Not all internalized racism affects mental health the same way
studies.ns_score_reason: a useful unpicking of a broad construct, but small, cross-sectional and incremental.
studies.the_study: A racially diverse sample of 205 US adults from racial and ethnic minority groups (mean age 28; 56% Black, 19% Asian, 15% multiracial) completed validated measures of internalized racism, anxiety and depression. Rather than treating internalized racism as one thing, the researchers separated four facets and tested each. Shame-based emotional reactions were tied specifically to anxious arousal, while devaluing one's own racial group — a cognitive rather than emotional process — was the facet linked to both anxiety and depressive symptoms.
studies.why_it_matters: If different components of internalized racism map onto different symptoms, the broad-brush measures used in most race-and-mental-health research are blurring effects that clinicians and researchers would do better to separate.
studies.pitch_angle: "Internalized racism" is usually measured as a single score; split it apart and only one piece — devaluing your own group — tracks with depression, while shame tracks with anxiety. The story is about the value of taking a broad psychological construct to bits. Call Jesus Quiles at Florida State University and press on whether these facets are separable in practice or just in a questionnaire's factor structure.
studies.wider_angle: A measurement-science feature for a general-interest or academic-culture outlet on how much of psychology's replication trouble comes from fuzzy constructs — grit, resilience, internalized stigma — that collapse several distinct processes into one number and one scale.
studies.caveats: Small N (205), cross-sectional and observational, all self-reported, convenience sample of US adults skewing young, no clinical diagnoses, effect sizes not reported in the abstract.

trends_raw:
**Convergent findings**
- **Breaking composite constructs into parts keeps producing the finding.** "Not all internalized racism affects mental health the same way" (PMID 42829217) splits a single questionnaire score into facets and finds shame tracks anxiety while group devaluation tracks depression — the same move that produced the previous digest's results on self-compassion, where uncompassionate self-responding did the explanatory work after stroke (PMID 42731412), on resilience, where forgiveness ran against every other item (PMID 42664566), and on social connection, where loneliness predicted depression and contact frequency predicted nothing (PMID 42623964).
- **Moderators, not main effects, carry the news.** "Whether war damages your mental health may depend on what you already believed about the world" (PMID 42844775) is this month's version of the pattern running through "Blood fat levels predict who responds to magnetic brain stimulation" (PMID 42720531) and "People whose brains respond least to reward gain most from a single mood-training session" (PMID 42700813): exposure or treatment alone explains little until you condition on who the person is.
- **Exercise keeps underdelivering on mood and cognition.** The aerobic arm of "Brain training for burnout still pays off four and a half years later" (PMID 42698289) showed no lasting cognitive advantage, adding to "Adding exercise to school PE lessons does nothing for teenagers' mood" (PMID 42752288). Two consecutive digests now in which a well-monitored exercise condition is the arm that does nothing.
- **Authors flagging their own confounds.** The Swedish team attributes its apparent long-term mood and work-ability gains to selective return rather than to treatment (PMID 42698289), which is the same self-policing seen last month in the Korean fertility claims analysis (PMID 42735740) and the active-comparator pregnancy cohort (PMID 42744942).

**Advances**
- **Neuromodulation moves from who responds to how fast.** Last month's TMS story was a sham-controlled trial hunting a response biomarker (PMID 42720531); this month "Rapid brain stimulation cuts suicidal thoughts within days in a small trial" (PMID 42842759) compresses the course into five days and targets suicidal ideation directly — a different axis of progress, though with no sham arm at all.
- **Bipolar and unipolar depression, from distinguishing to treating.** "Sleep and body-clock measures can tell unipolar and bipolar depression apart" (PMID 42751051) argued the two conditions are separable by objective markers; the accelerated iTBS study (PMID 42842759) reports that 17 bipolar and 17 unipolar inpatients responded about equally. Worth watching whether the distinction that matters for diagnosis matters for neuromodulation response.

**Counterpoints**
- **Design quality moves the wrong way.** The previous digest's neuromodulation entry was randomized and sham-controlled; this one is open-label with 34 patients and a 97% response rate (PMID 42842759). Against the deflationary run of the last two digests — null VR groups, null school exercise, vanishing drug-in-pregnancy signals — an uncontrolled 97% is a reminder of where those inflated effects come from in the first place.

**New themes**
- **Short-duration psychiatry.** "Short-acting psychedelics are being tested against depression — and one version leaves out the trip" (PMID 42838215) has no antecedent in the previous digest and pairs naturally with the five-day stimulation protocol. See below.
- **Civilian populations under active bombardment.** The previous digest reached conflict-affected people through refugees already in German treatment centers (PMID 42703887); PMID 42844775 samples parents during the crisis itself, six weeks in.
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Three of the five studies in this batch are about the clock. "Rapid brain stimulation cuts suicidal thoughts within days" (PMID 42842759) compresses six weeks of daily TMS visits into one five-day admission; "Short-acting psychedelics are being tested against depression" (PMID 42838215) reviews compounds whose acute effects resolve in 20 to 30 minutes, plus one engineered to skip the subjective experience entirely; and "Brain training for burnout still pays off four and a half years later" (PMID 42698289) is the mirror image — a few weeks of computerized training with a measurable cognitive trace nearly five years on. What links them is that the strength of the evidence runs inversely to the excitement: no sham arm in the stimulation trial, animal-only data for the non-hallucinogenic candidate, and 56 of 132 participants returning for the long follow-up.

**Why pitch this now:** The practical bottleneck in depression care has never been the drug or the coil, it has been the eight-hour supervised session and the six-week wait for an antidepressant to bite — and both are being engineered away at once, in trials that are too small or too uncontrolled to say whether the compressed version works.

**Angle:** A reported piece on how psychiatric treatment is being redesigned around duration — of the session, of the course, of the effect — and what evidence standards a five-day or twenty-minute intervention actually needs before health systems pay for it. For general readers who have been told to wait weeks for relief, with enough on trial design to show why "97% responded" and "no control group" belong in the same sentence.

**Potential headlines:**
- Depression treatments are getting shorter while the trials behind them get weaker
- The fast-acting psychiatric treatments nobody has yet tested against a placebo
- Patients in crisis are being offered week-long treatments built on studies with no comparison group

**Potential outlets:**
- **New Scientist Features** — the batch supports a long read on treatment duration and evidence thresholds rather than any single result, with the accelerated iTBS and short-acting tryptamine strands as the narrative spine.
- **STAT** — accelerated TMS protocols, inpatient throughput and reimbursement, plus the industry ties around non-hallucinogenic psychedelic development, sit directly in their coverage.
- **Undark** — well suited to the methodological core: open-label response rates, selective attrition, and what gets lost when a field optimizes for speed.
- **Wired** — the "engineer the trip out of the psychedelic" storyline, and the patent race it implies, fits their drug-development and biotech reporting.

# Fact-Check Report: New Scientist Story Ideas — Depression — October 2026
**Checked:** 2026-10-08 | **Studies reviewed:** 5
**Publication:** New Scientist | **Section:** New Scientist Mind

---

# Fact-Check Report — New Scientist Mind digest (run date 2026-10-08)

---

### Study 1: Brain training for burnout still pays off four and a half years later
**PMID:** 42698289 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Core facts check out: 132 randomized, 56 returned at 4.5 years, CCT group sustained effects on the global cognitive score, a trained updating task and episodic memory, AT group no extended cognitive benefit, and the psychological/work-ability gains attributed by the authors to selective attrition. Journal, volume, issue, article number and DOI all match.

**Issue A. Unstated training dose** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "burnout patients who did a few weeks of computerized training were still measurably sharper"
- **Abstract says:** Describes "the addition of computerised cognitive training (CCT) and aerobic training (AT) to a multimodal rehabilitation programme (MMR)" with no duration given.
- **Problem:** The length of the training course ("a few weeks", and "a short course" in Why it matters) is not verifiable from the abstract. If the original trial used a 12-week programme, "a few weeks" understates the intervention and inflates the hook.
- **Suggested fix:** "burnout patients who added computerised cognitive training to their rehabilitation were still measurably sharper" (and check the original trial protocol before specifying a duration).

**Issue B. "Among the longest follow-ups" claim** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "this is among the longest follow-ups showing that a short course of computerized training may leave a durable trace"
- **Abstract says:** Describes a 4.5-year follow-up but makes no priority or comparative claim.
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only; it is a literature-wide claim the abstract does not support. The "Novelty: First-in-class" tag rests on the same unverified comparison.
- **Suggested fix:** "this is an unusually long follow-up for a cognitive-training trial, showing…" — or source the claim from the authors on the record.

**Issue C. Author first name not in abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Call Hanna Malmberg Gavelin at Umeå University"
- **Abstract says:** "Gavelin HM(1)(6). (1)Department of Psychology, Umeå University, Umeå, Sweden."
- **Problem:** The full given name is unverifiable from abstract only. Affiliation and last-author status are correct.
- **Suggested fix:** Confirm the full name against the published paper or institutional page before the pitch goes out.

**Issue D. NS fit score** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "NS fit: 7/10 — a rare, very long follow-up of a randomized trial in burnout patients, dented by heavy attrition."
- **Problem:** A 7 is borderline here. The design is randomized and the primary outcome is objective cognitive testing, which supports a higher score than the other entries — but 58% of the original sample was lost, the per-group N at follow-up is very small, and the authors themselves discount a chunk of the results as attrition artefact. The score note is honest about this, but 7 slightly over-rewards it.
- **Suggested fix:** Score 6/10, with the same justification text.

---

### Study 2: Rapid brain stimulation cuts suicidal thoughts within days in a small trial
**PMID:** 42842759 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Response/remission at end of treatment (97.1%/73.5%), the 17/17 unipolar-bipolar split, daily C-SSRS assessment, the five-day protocol and the no-significant-difference-between-groups finding are all accurately reported.

**Issue A. "Inpatients" is not in the abstract** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Thirty-four inpatients with depression — 17 unipolar, 17 bipolar"
- **Abstract says:** "Thirty-four patients with depression (17 unipolar, 17 bipolar) completed a 5-day iTBS treatment protocol."
- **Problem:** The abstract never specifies inpatient status. This is not a cosmetic detail: it carries into the caveat ("inpatient sample may not generalize") and underpins the entire wider angle about "psychiatric inpatient care" and "compressing six weeks of daily hospital visits into one admission." If the sample was outpatient or mixed, that angle loses its peg.
- **Suggested fix:** "Thirty-four patients with depression — 17 unipolar, 17 bipolar" and verify setting from the full text before building the inpatient-care angle.

**Issue B. One-month response rounded down** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "at one month, roughly three-quarters still met response criteria"
- **Abstract says:** "At the one-month follow-up, response rates for suicidal ideation were 80% in the unipolar group and 75% in the bipolar group."
- **Problem:** "Roughly three-quarters" understates the unipolar figure and obscures that the rates were reported separately by group, not pooled.
- **Suggested fix:** "at one month, 80% of unipolar and 75% of bipolar patients still met response criteria, with remission maintained in about 60% of each group."

**Issue C. Single-centre and open-label described as fact** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "single center, open-label so expectancy effects are uncontrolled"
- **Abstract says:** No affiliations, country or blinding information are given; the methods describe a single treated cohort with no comparator.
- **Problem:** Absence of a sham arm is a fair inference from the methods, but "single center" and the explicit open-label designation are unverifiable from abstract only. Country of origin is also absent, which matters for the health-policy/insurance angle.
- **Suggested fix:** "no control or sham group reported; blinding and study setting not specified in the abstract; short follow-up (one month)."

**Issue D. "First-in-class" novelty label** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Novelty: First-in-class"
- **Abstract says:** "Intermittent theta-burst stimulation (iTBS) has emerged as a promising neuromodulatory technique with potential anti-suicidal and antidepressant effects."
- **Problem:** The abstract positions iTBS within an existing literature rather than as a first. Accelerated iTBS for suicidality has been trialled elsewhere; what may be novel here is the unipolar/bipolar comparison. The digest's own line that including bipolar patients "is unusual" is also unverifiable from the abstract.
- **Suggested fix:** "Novelty: New population (bipolar patients included in an accelerated iTBS protocol)".

---

### Study 3: Short-acting psychedelics are being tested against depression — and one version leaves out the trip
**PMID:** 42838215 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Fifty-one publications, 20–30 minute IV DMT acute effects, ~28 minute sublingual 5-MeO-DMT elimination half-life, GH001 meeting its Phase 2b primary endpoint, and zalsupindole's single preclinical study with no head-twitch response are all reported correctly. Crucially, the digest correctly preserves the abstract's hedge that zalsupindole's "human efficacy and hallucinogenic potential remain unknown," and the caveats disclose McIntyre's Atai Life Sciences and wider pharmaceutical ties as declared. Good practice.

**Issue A. Conflating route of administration with duration** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Lead on the contrast between a day-long psilocybin session and a 20-minute inhalation."
- **Abstract says:** "Intravenous N,N-DMT exhibited rapid pharmacokinetics, with acute effects resolving within 20-30 min, while sublingual 5-MeO-DMT had an elimination half-life of approximately 28 min. … GH001, an inhalable 5-MeO-DMT formulation…"
- **Problem:** The 20–30 minute figure belongs to intravenous DMT; the ~28 minute half-life belongs to sublingual 5-MeO-DMT. No duration is given for the inhaled GH001 formulation. The pitch merges all three into "a 20-minute inhalation."
- **Suggested fix:** "Lead on the contrast between a day-long psilocybin session and an intravenous dose whose effects resolve inside half an hour."

**Issue B. Eight-hour session figure not from the study** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "The practical obstacle to psychedelic therapy is the eight-hour supervised session"
- **Abstract says:** Refers only to "pharmacological profiles that may offer practical advantages over longer-acting psychedelics," with no session duration.
- **Problem:** Plausible background, but unverifiable from abstract only and presented in the Why it matters as if it came from the paper.
- **Suggested fix:** "The practical obstacle to psychedelic therapy is the long supervised session" — or attribute the eight-hour figure to a separate source.

**Issue C. "New mechanism" novelty label** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Novelty: New mechanism"
- **Abstract says:** "This systematic review aimed to synthesize pharmacological, clinical, safety, and preclinical behavioural evidence for these compounds."
- **Problem:** A systematic review synthesising existing evidence does not establish a new mechanism; the abstract explicitly lists dissociating neuroplasticity from hallucinogenic effects as an open question for future work.
- **Suggested fix:** "Novelty: Synthesis / emerging question".

---

### Study 4: Whether war damages your mental health may depend on what you already believed about the world
**PMID:** 42844775 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=326, parents of at least one child aged 3–6, mean age 36.75 (correctly rounded to 36.8), six weeks after the onset of the war, moderation by world assumptions, depression and somatization outcomes, and Greenblatt-Kimron's University of Haifa affiliation all match.

**Issue A. Headline and pitch imply pre-existing beliefs that were never measured** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Whether war damages your mental health may depend on what you already believed about the world" / "this study points at the reason: their prior assumptions about whether the world is fundamentally benign"
- **Abstract says:** "Participants completed questionnaires on background information, exposure to missile attacks, world assumptions, depression, and somatization six weeks after the onset of the Israel-Hamas war."
- **Problem:** World assumptions were measured concurrently with symptoms, six weeks into the war. The words "already believed," "prior assumptions" and "pre-existing beliefs" (in Why it matters) assert a temporal ordering the design cannot support — and directly contradict the digest's own caveat, "no baseline measures of pre-war beliefs or mood." "Points at the reason" also edges into causal language for a cross-sectional moderation analysis. The pitch's closing question partly rescues this, but the headline and setup have already made the claim.
- **Suggested fix:** Headline: "How badly war affects your mental health may track with how you see the world." Pitch: "this study points at one correlate: how benign they believe the world to be, measured alongside their symptoms rather than before the war."

**Issue B. "Far weaker" link in the positive-assumptions group** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "among those with more positive assumptions, the link was far weaker"
- **Abstract says:** "Findings of the moderation analyses revealed a strong positive relationship between exposure to missile attacks with symptoms of depression and somatization among parents holding negative world assumptions."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports the high-negative-assumption simple slope only. A weaker association at the other end is the usual implication of a moderation, but the abstract does not state its magnitude or whether it was significant, so "far weaker" overspecifies.
- **Suggested fix:** "the association was strongest among parents holding negative world assumptions; the abstract does not report the size of the association among those with more positive assumptions."

**Issue C. Sample described as a convenience sample** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "non-probability online convenience sample"
- **Abstract says:** "A web-based national sample included 326 parents with at least one child aged 3-6 years."
- **Problem:** The abstract calls it a national web-based sample; whether recruitment was non-probability is unverifiable from abstract only. The caveat errs on the cautious side, which is preferable to the reverse, but it misstates what the paper claims.
- **Suggested fix:** "web-based national sample; recruitment method not specified in the abstract."

**Issue D. "Counterintuitive" novelty label** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Novelty: Counterintuitive"
- **Abstract says:** Frames the study as testing "the moderating role of world assumptions," i.e. an application of existing shattered-assumptions theory.
- **Problem:** The finding — that negative world assumptions amplify the stress–symptom link — is the direction the underlying theory predicts. Nothing in the abstract is counterintuitive.
- **Suggested fix:** "Novelty: Theory tested in a live conflict setting".

---

### Study 5: Not all internalized racism affects mental health the same way
**PMID:** 42829217 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Demographics are accurately rounded (N=205; mean age 27.96 → 28; 55.6% → 56% Black; 18.5% → 19% Asian; 14.6% → 15% multiracial), the four-facet structure is correctly described, and the split finding — affective/shame facets with anxious arousal, group devaluation with both anxiety and depression — matches the abstract. The digest appropriately declines to echo the abstract's clinical implications about cognitive restructuring, which would not be supportable from cross-sectional data. The 4/10 NS fit score is well calibrated.

**Issue A. Author first name not in abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Call Jesus Quiles at Florida State University"
- **Abstract says:** "Quiles JRG(1)… (1)Department of Psychology, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL, USA"
- **Problem:** First name unverifiable from abstract only (the listed contact email is garcia@psy.fsu.edu, and the surname may be compound). Affiliation is correct.
- **Suggested fix:** Confirm the preferred full name and surname form from the published paper before contacting.

---

## Issue Summary

| Study # | Headline | Verdict | Notes |
|---------|----------|---------|-------|
| 1 | Brain training for burnout still pays off four and a half years later | ⚠️ Minor issues | Unverified training duration and "longest follow-up" claim; NS fit 7 → suggest 6 |
| 2 | Rapid brain stimulation cuts suicidal thoughts within days in a small trial | ⚠️ Minor issues | "Inpatients" not in abstract and drives the wider angle; one-month response rates rounded down |
| 3 | Short-acting psychedelics are being tested against depression | ⚠️ Minor issues | Route/duration conflated in pitch; novelty label wrong for a review; COI disclosure handled well |
| 4 | Whether war damages your mental health may depend on what you already believed | ⚠️ Minor issues | Headline/pitch assert pre-war beliefs that were measured concurrently, contradicting own caveat |
| 5 | Not all internalized racism affects mental health the same way | ⚠️ Minor issues | Statistically and framing-accurate; author first name unverifiable |

**Total issues:** 16 (14 Minor, 2 Moderate, 0 Major)
**Entries requiring revision:** 5
**Entries cleared:** 0

**Editor's note on patterns:** Two recurring habits account for most of the flags. First, contextual detail not present in the abstracts (training duration, inpatient status, single-centre design, eight-hour psilocybin sessions) is being presented in the same register as verified study facts — each of these needs either full-text sourcing or hedging before the pitch goes out. Second, the novelty labels are running ahead of the abstracts in three of five entries. On the plus side, the caveats sections are generally strong, industry funding in Study 3 is properly surfaced, and no entry converts observational or uncontrolled findings into a clinical recommendation. Study 4's headline is the single item I would hold until rewritten.
